summary: Gives recommendations for randomizing transport-protocol port numbers to defend against blind attacks on TCP and similar protocols. Such attacks rely on guessing the connection five-tuple, and randomizing the ephemeral port makes this harder.

plainLanguage.summary: When a program opens a connection, its networking stack chooses a temporary source port. RFC 6056 describes ways to make that choice harder for an off-path attacker to guess, while limiting reuse that can disrupt connections.

questions: how do hosts pick random source ports
what port range should ephemeral ports use
subtitle: How transport stacks can make automatically chosen client ports harder to predict.

tldr.problem: Blind attacks can target a transport connection if an attacker can guess its five-tuple. A sequential client-port counter makes the source port easy to predict.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five methods for obfuscating ephemeral-port selection, balancing unpredictability against port reuse and collisions. It recommends using the largest available range, from 1024 through 65535.
tldr.outcome: Port selection can be changed locally and incrementally, but it does not protect against an attacker who can observe packets and does not replace cryptographic protection. RFC 6056 is BCP 156.

today: RFC 6056 is Best Current Practice (BCP 156), published in January 2011. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How a Port Helps Identify a Connection
sections.content:
A transport connection is identified by a five-tuple: protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port. Blind attacks on TCP and similar protocols try to guess that tuple without seeing the packets. Their effects can range from reduced throughput to broken connections or corrupted data.

A server normally uses a known service port. When a client does not choose its own port, the networking stack selects an ephemeral port. Making that port harder to predict can reduce the chance of a successful off-path guess. It does not protect against an attacker who can observe the traffic and is not a replacement for cryptographic mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The client port is one value an off-path attacker may need to guess to target a connection. Choosing it unpredictably can make that attack harder, but it cannot hide the port from someone watching the packets.

sections.title: Ephemeral Ports and Reuse
sections.content:
IANA divides the 16-bit TCP and UDP port range into well-known ports 0-1023, registered ports 1024-49151 and dynamic or private ports 49152-65535. RFC 6056 says selection algorithms should use the wider range 1024-65535, excluding ports needed by local services.

A traditional algorithm keeps a shared next-port counter and advances it for each connection. This avoids reusing a port until the range has been traversed, but an observer who learns one port can often predict later choices and estimate how many connections were opened. Purely random selection hides the sequence better but may reuse a five-tuple while a remote endpoint still remembers it.
sections.plainLanguage: A counter avoids some rapid port reuse but makes the next choice predictable. Random choices are harder to predict, but can reuse a connection identifier too soon.

sections.title: What a Port-Selection Algorithm Must Balance
sections.content:
A good algorithm aims to make future ports hard to predict, minimize collisions between connection identifiers and avoid ports that applications require for specific services. The RFC uses the term obfuscation for reducing an attacker's ability to guess, not producing mathematically random sequences.

Port choices must avoid tuples already in use locally. A tuple may also remain in TIME-WAIT at the remote endpoint after the local connection closes, so reusing it can cause connection failures or other problems. The algorithm should also avoid ports used by TCP sockets in LISTEN or, for some APIs, CLOSED state.

The RFC recommends the largest possible port range and a local list of ports that services on the host need. Administrators should exclude only registered ports used by local services, rather than excluding every registered port.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm must make ports hard to guess without reusing connection identifiers too quickly. It must also leave ports available for services running on the same host.

sections.title: Five Ways to Obfuscate Port Choices
sections.content:
Algorithm 1 chooses a random starting port and scans forward for a suitable port. Algorithm 2 chooses a fresh random port after each collision. Both are simple, but random selection can increase collisions; Algorithm 1 can become biased when many ports are unavailable.

Algorithm 3 uses a keyed hash of the local address, remote address and remote port to choose a destination-specific offset, then advances a counter. Algorithm 4 adds a second hash to select among a table of counters, reducing shared increments at the cost of processing and memory. Algorithm 5 advances a counter by a random increment from 1 to N, balancing predictability and port reuse according to the value of N.
sections.plainLanguage: Some methods pick ports at random; others use a secret hash to start separate sequences for different destinations. A fifth method takes random-sized steps, with its setting controlling the balance between surprise and reuse.

sections.title: Secret Keys for Hash-Based Selection
sections.content:
Algorithms 3 and 4 depend on secret keys used by their hash functions. If an attacker knows the function and collects enough selected ports, the attacker may search for the key. RFC 6056 says a key length of 128 bits should be adequate and points to RFC 4086 for choosing random secrets.

Changing the key changes the offset used for destinations, which may cause a recently used port to be selected again. The RFC says to change it with care, such as when few transport instances are active or enough real random data is available. Pseudo-random key changes should not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Hash-based methods need a secret that is difficult to guess. Changing it can make a recently used port appear available again, so the change needs to account for active connections.

sections.title: Choosing Among the Algorithms
sections.content:
An empirical study cited by the RFC found collision rates of at most 0.3% for the tested scenarios, but results may vary with traffic and network setup. The first two algorithms had the highest collision rates in that study. Hash-based methods reduce reuse or improve separation but require extra computation; Algorithm 4 also needs table memory.

Algorithms 3 and 4 need the remote address and port to calculate their hash. If an application binds to port zero before those values are known, the hash cannot yet be computed. The RFC suggests considering Algorithm 2 for that case or delaying port selection until the application connects or sends.
sections.plainLanguage: Each method has a different cost in computation, memory, predictability and port reuse. A system also needs to check when its applications provide enough connection details to calculate a hash.

sections.title: Network Address and Port Translation
sections.content:
A Network Address Port Translator (NAPT) changes addresses and port numbers, so the external port may be selected by the translator rather than the client. The RFC recommends that NAPTs consider obfuscating ports when they change them.

Some applications expect a sequence of contiguous ports. Random selection methods can break that expectation, while Algorithms 3 and 4 select consecutive ports except when a required port is already in use. The RFC warns that applications relying on a particular NAPT selection method may have interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator may choose the port visible to the remote server. It should use an unpredictable choice when it changes a port, while considering applications that expect consecutive ports.

sections.title: Limits of Port Obfuscation
sections.content:
Port obfuscation does not replace cryptographic protection such as IPsec. An eavesdropper can observe the addresses, ports and other connection information and can attack without guessing the source port.

Algorithm 1 may be highly biased if the unavailable-port list is large. The RFC says systems with many unavailable ports, or systems that exclude the IANA Registered Ports list without modification, must not use Algorithm 1. Hash-based algorithms also depend on an offset function that does not produce too many identical results for different inputs.
sections.plainLanguage: Port selection only makes guessing harder for attackers who cannot see the traffic. Use cryptographic protection when the connection also needs protection from an observer.
